content.text:
This wasn't a normal file open. `source-unavailable.3mf` is the placeholder file name JusPrin uses when it reloads one of its own saved project checkpoints. That checkpoint-reload path doesn't use the dialog suppression that file opens get.

**How suppression works.** Every Orca dialog goes through `answer_modal` before it is shown. A dialog is answered automatically only while a listener is active:
- **Your file opens** (File › Open, drag and drop, recent files): `file_open_started` installs a listener that answers every dialog, in [OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:709](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:709). This is the rule you remembered.
- **Agent tool calls**: they install the same kind of listener.
- **Checkpoint reloads**: these call `plater.load_files` directly, through `load_managed_checkpoint` in [ProjectAutosave.cpp:107](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:107). That function's only listener answers the dialog titled "Modified G-code" and nothing else. Commit e3f826a83c (2026-10-07) did this on purpose. Its comment says it keeps "every other restore dialog" visible. Three actions take this path: resuming the last project at launch (`resume_latest`), opening a project from Home (`open_managed_project`), and reverting to a checkpoint (`restore_impl`).

**Why you got "Customized Preset" and not "Modified G-code".** Both warnings come from the same block in Orca's 3MF loader ([Plater.cpp:6388-6412](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6388)), and they are two branches of one check:
- "Modified G-code" appears when the project's presets exist locally but their G-code was edited.
- "Customized Preset" appears when a preset named in the project can't be found locally as a system preset (or one inheriting from a system preset).

I checked the latest checkpoint of this project on disk (`~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/projects/p-695f6cbd7c153ebf-6d45f33818b087a0/versions/1793049154180-daf1f49b646ff6bf/metadata.3mf`). It stores:
- `filament_settings_id`: `Bambu PLA Basic @BBL P1S 0.4 nozzle(find_my_hollow.3mf)`, three times
- `inherits_group`: missing

The `(find_my_hollow.3mf)` suffix is how Orca names a preset that only exists inside an imported project. When the checkpoint is reloaded, no preset by that name is installed. With `inherits_group` missing, `PresetCollection::validate_preset` also can't fall back to the parent preset, `Bambu PLA Basic @BBL P1S 0.4 nozzle`. So the check fails, and nothing answers the dialog.

When you first opened `find_my_hollow.3mf`, the same warning most likely fired and was answered silently by the file-open listener. So on every reload this is the same false alarm that e3f826a83c already suppresses for "Modified G-code". It just takes the other branch.

**Two things I haven't verified:**
- Which of the three actions you took. The app's log on disk is months old, so it can't tell me.
- Why `inherits_group` is missing from the checkpoint. I'd expect a project saved by Orca to include it. If the checkpoint writer drops it, keeping it might be the better fix than suppressing one more dialog title.

Ticking "Don't show again" in that dialog turns off both warnings for every project, because they share the `no_warn_when_modified_gcodes` setting.
Is it fair to say that your diagnosis that some upstream dialogs are still not surppressed? If so, can you list all of them?

Yes, that's fair, with one narrowing. Opening a file yourself, through any route, auto-answers every Orca dialog. Some Orca dialogs still reach the screen when JusPrin reloads one of its own saved checkpoints. All of this comes from reading the code. I haven't reproduced anything beyond the dialog in your screenshot.

**A correction to my last answer.** I said checkpoint reloads skip the dialog hook because they call `load_files` directly. The hook actually sits inside Orca's own `load_files` ([Plater.cpp:5877](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:5877)), so every load reaches it. JusPrin's handler then skips loads on purpose ([OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:652-658](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:652)): loads marked "silent" and settings-only loads. Checkpoint reloads use Orca's `Restore` load mode, which includes the silent flag. The outcome is the same as I described: apart from the one "Modified G-code" exception, nothing answers dialogs during a checkpoint reload.

**Which loads are covered**

| How the load starts | Dialogs auto-answered? |
|---|---|
| File › Open, Cmd+O, drag and drop, recent files, Add model, Home's open, MakerWorld import, startup files | Yes, the whole open, including Orca's pre-load questions such as "save changes?" |
| Agent tool calls (`project_open`, `object_import_file`, and others) | Yes |
| Orca's own crash recovery (`load_project` with a backup file) | Yes for the load itself. The "Previous unsaved project detected, restore it?" question before it is not covered. |
| **JusPrin checkpoint reloads**: launch resume, opening a project from Home, revert ([ProjectAutosave.cpp:107](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:107)) | **No**, except "Modified G-code" |
| Import config from project (Orca's settings-only import) | No. This is skipped on purpose as a settings-only load. |

**Orca dialogs that can still appear during a checkpoint reload**

All of these are in `Plater::priv::load_files`. The silent flag only stops Orca from remembering the folder. It doesn't hide any dialog.

Likely to fire on a checkpoint:
1. **"Customized Preset"** ([Plater.cpp:6408](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6408)): the one you saw. It fires whenever the project uses a preset that only exists inside an imported project, such as `…(find_my_hollow.3mf)`.
2. **"Tips: Connected printer is X. It must match the project preset… sync?"** ([Plater.cpp:6905](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6905)): fires if a Bambu printer is connected and doesn't match the project's printer preset, unless you ticked its "don't show again" box before.
3. **Load errors** (`show_error`, [Plater.cpp:6679-6683](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6679)): with nothing listening, Orca shows an error dialog after the load ends.
4. **The "Loading…" progress window** ([Plater.cpp:5914](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:5914)). It asks nothing, but it appears for every load, covered or not, because it is a plain wx progress window that never goes through the hook. It was the window behind the dialog in your screenshot.

Possible but unlikely, because a checkpoint is a current-version 3MF that JusPrin wrote itself:

5. "Load 3MF" / "Newer 3MF version" / "BambuStudio Project" version notices ([Plater.cpp:6074-6204](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6074))
6. "Infill rotation template… clear it?" for projects made in OrcaSlicer 2.3.1-alpha ([Plater.cpp:6093](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6093), [6148](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6148))
7. "The file does not contain any geometry data" ([Plater.cpp:7039](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:7039)). Checkpoint reloads pass the allow-empty flag when the project has no objects, so this one should not fire.

Fire only when importing a mesh, not a project, so a checkpoint should never trigger them: "Objects with zero volume removed", "Object too small… scale to millimeters?", "load as a single object with multiple parts?", the OBJ colour dialog, and the STEP import settings.

**What I didn't cover.** I only traced loading. Other flows still show Orca dialogs too, for example "save changes?" when you start a new project from Home, and the crash-recovery question in the table. I also checked how each dialog is displayed: every question dialog in this load code goes through the hook, so none of them would slip past a listener if one were active. The progress window is the only exception.

I haven't made the fix the other session passed on from you ([File open dialog suppression](#local_6fd445db-0b28-4341-96de-73daf522ca1b)), because it rests on a wrong guess. The checkpoint doesn't drop the preset's parent. That parent doesn't exist in JusPrin, so there's nothing to keep.

**What I checked**
- **JusPrin has no preset by that name.** No preset called `Bambu PLA Basic @BBL P1S 0.4 nozzle` exists in `resources/profiles/BBL/` or in the system profiles installed in your data folder. On a P1S with a 0.4 nozzle, the BBL profiles use `Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C`, and no rename or alias maps the P1S name onto it.
- **The original file has the same problem.** `~/Downloads/find_my_hollow.3mf` was written by Bambu Studio (its version field is 02.06.00.51). Its filaments are named `Bambu PLA Basic @BBL P1S 0.4 nozzle` and it has no `inherits_group`. So Orca's check already failed when you first opened it. JusPrin's file-open listener answered OK without showing you anything, and the warning text went into the agent's load report.
- **The checkpoint is a faithful copy.** After that first open, Orca created a filament preset that exists only inside this project, `…(find_my_hollow.3mf)`, with no parent. The checkpoint stores exactly that, so nothing changes between save and reload. Orca's check trusts only system, default and bundle presets, so it fails on every reload of this project. The same would happen to any project whose presets came from Bambu Studio and don't exist in JusPrin.

**The decision.** Every reload of such a project will show this dialog until one of these changes. The choice is yours because it changes how Orca's G-code safety warning applies:

1. **Treat the check as answered at open, and skip it on checkpoint reloads.** The checkpoint is JusPrin's own copy of a file that already went through the check when it was opened. This is the same approach e3f826a83c took for "Modified G-code". The catch: "answered" means JusPrin answered it automatically at open; no person ever saw the warning. That part is unchanged either way. **This is my recommendation**, because no save/reload mismatch exists to fix at its source.
2. **Give the preset a parent at open time.** When a foreign preset's name isn't installed, match it to one that is, for example by filament ID plus printer, so the project's preset gets a parent and checkpoints store it. This changes how Orca imports projects from Bambu Studio, in files Orca owns. It costs effort at every rebase, and it guesses a parent that the file never named.
3. **Leave it.** The dialog stays on every reload of these projects.

content.text:
Yes, the "Modified G-code" suppression is hacky, and reusing it for "Customized Preset" would add a second copy of the same hack. I read your question as "should we handle this the same way as the G-code warning, given that mechanism is hacky?" If you meant something else, tell me.

**Why the existing suppression is hacky** (from commit e3f826a83c, in `load_managed_checkpoint`, [ProjectAutosave.cpp:117](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:117)):
- **It matches on the dialog's title words.** It answers any dialog whose title equals the translated "Modified G-code". JusPrin's own listener design says not to do that: [DialogListeners.hpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/DialogListeners.hpp) states that "Nothing is matched against the words". If Orca rewords the title, the suppression silently stops working.
- **It hides a false alarm JusPrin created.** Commit 1fcc7e05a4 makes checkpoints mark every captured setting as owned by the project. Orca's check reads that as "every G-code setting differs from the system preset". The suppression hides that symptom; the cause is still there.
- **It intercepts the dialog after Orca has built it.** It doesn't stop the check from running.

**A cleaner fix for both warnings.** Both dialogs come from one block in Orca's 3MF loader ([Plater.cpp:6381](src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6381)), which Orca already skips when you tick "Don't warn when loading 3MF with modified G-code" in Preferences. Two load paths use Orca's `Restore` load mode: Orca's own crash-backup restore and JusPrin's checkpoint reloads. Adding one condition to that block, skip the check when the load is a `Restore`, would:
- stop both "Modified G-code" and "Customized Preset" on checkpoint reloads, with no text matching and no dialog built
- let us delete the title-matching listener from e3f826a83c
- also stop Orca's crash-backup restore from re-warning. That is defensible, since a backup is the app's own copy of a file it already checked, but it changes upstream behavior in a file Orca owns. It needs the rebase notes required by `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`.

I also considered switching that Orca preference on temporarily during a checkpoint reload, which would need no Orca edit. I'd avoid it. Orca writes the app config to disk on idle while it is dirty, and the loading progress window lets idle events run during the load. So the temporary setting could be saved, and it would stay on if the app crashed mid-load.

One related item, whichever fix you pick: the checkpoint writer listing every setting as different from the system preset is still a real save/reload mismatch. Skipping the check on restore makes it harmless for this warning. I haven't checked whether anything else reads that list.

All of this comes from reading the code. Before changing anything, I'd reproduce the dialog in the shell harness using this project's checkpoint.

name: pkill-cmake-build-leaves-ninja

On 2026-10-21 Kenneth found 4 Release builds and 56 clang processes on 12 cores, all mine, in one worktree. Every ninja ran at its default -j (cores + 2), so 4 × 14 = 56. He pointed out that the orphaned processes were the smaller problem. The bigger one was that I put that many builds there at all.

What I did wrong, in order of weight:
1. I treated builds as free on a machine other sessions build on too. I never passed `-j`. I saw load 33, then 76, and started more builds anyway.
2. I restarted the build three times to change its target list or to slip in a small target. Each restart cost a full set of jobs. Waiting for the running build and adding targets afterwards cost nothing.
3. I went against the brief ("reuse the existing build; another session may be building") by configuring a fresh full-app build for an optional live check.
4. I blamed the slowness on "other sessions" without counting my own processes. That is the plausible-story-instead-of-checking failure from CLAUDE.md.
5. Mechanism: `pkill -f "cmake --build <dir>"` kills only the wrapper. Its `ninja -C <dir>` child keeps compiling as an orphan. I never checked that a stop had worked.

**Why:** the machine is shared. My extra jobs slow every other session, and two ninjas in one build dir can leave its records inconsistent.

**How to apply:**
- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. Cap jobs with `-- -j4` (fewer when load is above the core count).
- Decide the full target list once. Never restart a build to change it.
- Run one build per dir as its own process group (`set -m`, then kill with `kill -- -<pgid>`). After any stop, confirm with `pgrep -fl "ninja.*<dir>"`.
- Ask before a full-app build that the task did not require.

Related: [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

184 agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md
# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

The rules above still apply. For this one response, write the first message about the file just opened or imported, by the person or by a tool call of mine. Report and offer from the report and the picture, and change nothing the person has not asked for.

The report separates four sources. The app-computed opening outcome (loadFacts, loads, and objects) establishes what was loaded and how the selected printer, material and print settings changed. A load's withSettings only says the app requested settings, not that it applied them; claim they were applied only when loadFacts.settingsOutcome says applied. If that outcome is absent, leave the application of settings uncertain. The current workspace establishes what is selected now; setupPrinters lists printer models the person has set up in JusPrin, each with bedMm, its bed's width, depth and printable height; selectedPrinterBedMm is the selected printer's. For each object, placedOnBed says whether it sits wholly on the bed now, clear of any area the printer's profile excludes, and fitsSelectedBed and fitsSetupPrinters whether its size fits each bed somewhere, turned a quarter-turn if needed: an object that is off the bed but fits it needs moving, not resizing. mesh is the app's check of the model: shells is how many separate pieces it is made of, openEdges or repairedErrors above zero mean holes or errors in it, and unitsSuspicion says when its size looks like inches or metres. customized lists what the file already prepared for printing: painted supports, seams, colours or fuzzy skin, and its own layer heights. fileFacts is what each 3MF says about itself: the app that saved it, the printer and nozzle it was made for, and its filaments. Neither a selection nor that list proves which physical machine they intend to use. The raw messages.items contain Orca's dialog title and text, offered buttons, and the answer JusPrin supplied automatically. The person did not choose that answer and may never have seen the dialog. The file's details.description and details.profileDescription are author notes: claims from the file, not proof that their advice was applied. The picture, when present, is the active plate after the load, rendered from the iso view.

Look at the attached picture when there is one. Check the selected printer, filament and process presets and the plate type against the file and against the printers the person has set up; when one looks wrong for this print, say which and suggest the one to use, without changing it. When an object does not fit the selected printer, name a set-up printer it fits, from fitsSetupPrinters.

Write about 80 words, with at most two bullets, about what matters for this file now. The person sees the setup card above your message, with the presets, the plate and the estimates, and the activity line under your turn, with the checks you made: leave those to them rather than restating them.
- Lead with what decides whether or how it can print: a load that failed, an object that does not fit, a printer to choose, settings or G-code that need review. Say it once, with only the numbers that matter.
- Say what you take the object to be, and how it should be printed, only when that changes the advice, and then briefly, as a guess. Leave other advice (material, strength, orientation) until the main decision is made.
- Do not explain routine loading: how the file was opened, whether its settings were applied, or which notices appeared, unless it changes the next step. Do not imply that loading the file ran G-code on a printer. Never claim a warning was fixed merely because its dialog was dismissed.
- When nothing needs attention, say so in a sentence.
- End with exactly one question, about the next step: the message's only question, not a menu of alternatives. Do not offer to print while the intended printer or another consequential choice is unresolved.

Read each actual notice with its automatic answer and the final opening outcome. The guide below is deliberately not a code classification table.

| Notice or event you may encounter | Importance and explanation for the person |
| --- | --- |
| A newer or partly incompatible 3MF asks whether to continue | If opening succeeded, mention a lost or changed feature only when the outcome shows one. If it failed, explain the failure. Omit a version warning with no consequence. |
| Settings were substituted with supported values | Usually omit when completed successfully. Explain briefly if the result materially changes the print or still needs a choice. |
| “Customized Preset” or a file setting has no installed match | This alone does not establish that machine commands changed. Use the final selected printer and material to judge the consequence. |
| “Modified G-code” | When the notice says so, the file includes modified G-code in its printer or filament settings, and I warned about it while opening the file. G-code is the instructions a printer runs. Name the affected setting if the notice gives it and that helps locate what to review; do not invent a line number or claim I inspected the commands. Explain that these instructions need review before printing, without claiming they are safe or unsafe. Offer to review the modified G-code next. |
| Invalid values in a 3MF | If the model loaded, say which file settings need checking when their names are supplied. Do not say they were corrected unless the outcome establishes that. |
| Zero-volume parts were removed | Mention omitted parts when they could change the intended model. If nothing usable remains, lead with the failed opening. |
| “Object too small” asks whether to scale | The recorded answer says whether JusPrin scaled it. If it stayed tiny, state its final numeric size and ask the intended size. If scaled, mention the conversion only if it matters. |
| “Object too large” asks whether to shrink | The answer and final dimensions say whether it was shrunk. If still too large, explain the bed-fit problem. If shrunk, explain that its intended size may have changed. |
| A choice to open a 3MF as a project or geometry only | Use loadFacts.settingsOutcome to say whether the file's print settings were applied. Explain only when it changes the next step. |
| Connected-printer synchronization | Use the final selection and separately supplied connection state. Do not infer a connected machine from a preset name. |
| OBJ colour mapping, STEP mesh options, or unreadable STEP names | Mention a resulting colour, shape, precision or naming problem only when it matters to this model. |
| Multiple parts or files become one object | Mention grouping only if it changes how the person can print or edit the model. |
| A suggestion to simplify a very detailed model | Usually omit from the first message unless a current performance or editing problem exists. |
| A refusal to mix G-code with models, open multiple G-code files, or add models in preview mode | If the requested file did not open, explain that directly and give the next useful step. |
| “File contains no geometry” or a loading error | Lead with what failed and what, if anything, was added. Give the actual reason when available; do not invent one. |

An alarming notice does not override the final outcome. An automatic “No”, “Yes” or “OK” is JusPrin's action, not the person's preference. If several issues matter, address the most important decision first and briefly flag another consequential issue for later. Do not turn an already completed change into a fresh action item.

Use useful file author advice only when it affects the next step; keep it secondary to an unresolved printer or size decision. Attribute it to the file.

That clears the mark on the setup card; nothing else does.

Write in uiLanguage when it is supplied. Keep it short.

input.title: Preset name grows "(.3mf)" on each checkpoint restore
input.prompt:
Find and fix why restoring a JusPrin checkpoint renames a project-only filament preset by appending "(.3mf)".

Observed in the workspace harness (`tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp`, `verify_unknown_preset_checkpoint`, on branch `claude/checkpoint-skip-preset-check`, worktree `.claude/worktrees/checkpoint-preset-check`): open a 3MF whose filament preset name is not installed and has no `inherits_group`. Orca creates the project-only preset `Harness PLA @Not Installed(unknown-preset.3mf)`. After `ProjectAutosave::restore` reloads a checkpoint, the selected filament is `Harness PLA @Not Installed(unknown-preset.3mf)(.3mf)`. The harness prints both names as `HARNESS UNKNOWN_PRESET_OPENED` and `HARNESS UNKNOWN_PRESET_RESTORED`.

Hypothesis, not verified: the checkpoint's materialized metadata file is literally named `.3mf` (`ProjectVersionStore::materialize`, `result.metadata = result.directory / ".3mf"`). Orca's `PresetCollection::load_external_preset` (`src/libslic3r/Preset.cpp`, around `new_name = prefix + "(" + name + ")"`) names a new project-only preset after the file it came from, so every restore adds another suffix. Check whether repeated restores keep growing the name, and whether resume at launch and opening a project from Home do the same.

Done means: reproduce it with a harness check first, fix it at the source in fork-owned code where possible (any Orca-file change follows `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`), make the check pass, and report what the person would have seen before and after. Do not commit unless Kenneth asks.
input.background: JusPrin is a fork of OrcaSlicer. It saves each project as checkpoints (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp`, `ProjectVersionStore.cpp`) and reloads them through `Plater::load_files` with `LoadStrategy::Restore`. Kenneth's rule: a checkpoint reload must feel like nothing happened, and any difference between what was saved and what reloads is a save/reload mismatch to fix at its source, not hide. The related fix on `claude/checkpoint-skip-preset-check` (uncommitted) makes Restore loads skip Orca's 3MF preset safety check. The harness binary there is built in Release at `build/arm64/tests/workspace/Release/JusPrinWorkspaceHarness.app`; 14 checks already fail before any change (second_model_dropped, model_added_to_a_project_is_an_edit, and 12 calibration identity checks). Build with `-- -j4` on this shared Mac.

content.text:
Checkpoint reloads (launch resume, opening a project from Home, revert) no longer show Orca's "Customized Preset" or "Modified G-code" dialogs. I removed the hacky title-matching suppression from commit e3f826a83c and replaced it with one condition in Orca's loader. The harness reproduced both dialogs before the change and shows neither after. Nothing is committed yet. The work is in its own worktree, `.claude/worktrees/checkpoint-preset-check`, on branch `claude/checkpoint-skip-preset-check`, because other sessions were committing in the main checkout.

**What changed**
- [Plater.cpp:6383](.claude/worktrees/checkpoint-preset-check/src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp:6383): Orca's 3MF preset safety check now also skips loads that use the `Restore` mode. That is one added condition and one comment line.
- [ProjectAutosave.cpp:107](.claude/worktrees/checkpoint-preset-check/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:107): the cleanup you asked for. The listener that answered any dialog titled "Modified G-code" is gone, along with its include. `load_managed_checkpoint` is now just the shared load call for the four checkpoint-reload paths, with a comment pointing to the Plater.cpp condition.
- [real_adapter_harness.cpp](.claude/worktrees/checkpoint-preset-check/tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp): a new check, `verify_unknown_preset_checkpoint`. It exports a project, rewrites it to name a filament preset that isn't installed and has no parent, opens it, saves a checkpoint, saves again, and restores the first checkpoint. It fails if any Orca dialog appears. The existing restore check stays and now uses a shared dialog recorder.

**How it was tested** (workspace harness, Release build)
